This article was written at a time when online education and using different technologies to 20 access educational materials from our homes came to the fore due to the COVID-19 pandemic. 21 From this context, many are aware that technology offers education a number of opportunities, in 22 terms of enhancing existing provisions, but also challenges such as creating inequalities (Howley 23 2021). Yet, in addressing this83 gap, we are conscious of the need to problematise TEL more generally in relation to questioning 84 what is 'enhanced' and how do we know it is enhanced? (Kirkwood & Price, 2014). Others go as 85 far as the need to problematize the very ontological underpinnings of TEL (Bayne, 2015). Whilst 86 it is beyond the scope of this paper to attend to the nature of these debates, there remains the 87 need to critically review what aspect of pedagogy is claimed to be enhanced using digital 88 technology. Furthermore, who is the subject of the claim of enhancement such as the teacher, 89 learner, or educational bodies. Attending to such areas addresses a notable gap in the field of PE 90 and sport pedagogy and will serve as a recognized source of information to inform future 91 research and decision making in relation to the use of digital technology in PE. Therefore, the 92 purpose of this paper is to critically review TEL in the PE literature with specific relationship to 93 the notion of pedagogy.

Search strategy and parametersLiterature was selected from searching the databases of Web of Science, Scopus, and Dialnet,110 through a title and abstract search procedure. Following Alexander (2020) directions these 111 database searches were limited to peer-reviewed publications that were published between 2015 112 and 2020. The main search keywords were a combination of both a technology based key word 113 and an identifier from PE in both the abstract and title. The search terms were used in both 114 English and Spanish. For example, some of the search terms we used were a combination of 115 'technology-enhanced learning' AND 'physical education', and 'physical education' AND 116 'digital technology' 1 . A manual search of the list of references of selected articles was also 117 performed, not resulting in the inclusion of more papers to the ones yielded through the database 118 search. 119 Inclusion and exclusion criteria 120 Given the authors backgrounds, this critical review considered empirical English and Spanish-121 language research undertaken between 2015 and 2020 that was published in print or digital 122 formats, in peer-reviewed articles relevant to the research question. The rationale for this 123 timeframe is to encompass five years of rapid technological development and the relatively 124 nuanced nature of the work on technology in the PE field, and the growing number of 125 technology-based interventions. This approach was chosen as it allowed the capturing 143 of the often iterate and nonlinear nature of reviews and to explore alternative paths to the 144 findings (Alexander, 2020). A two-stage approach to this critical review of the literature was 145 chosen to align with reviews such as Cushion and Townsend (2019) and to provide a semi-146 structured approach. The first stage involved mining the databases using our inclusion/exclusion 147 criteria. Prior to individual coding, we completed a sub-sample of papers together to establish 148 consistency between our approaches. Then, the authors individually reviewed and coded the title 149 and abstracts, using Rayyan website tool for systematic reviews. The coding was then compared 150 between the authors and any points of clarity or conflicts were discussed and agreed. The second 151 'quality screening phase' involved a creation of a descriptive matrix of the literature to provide a 152 map of the TEL field (Cushion et al., 2010; Cushion & Townsend, 2019). The initial map 153 involved reading and filtering the full articles in terms of the article focus (and coverage) of 154 technology (e.g., the platform, device, software of study) and the three areas of teaching (e.g., a 155 detailed description of the intervention), learning (e.g., evidence of learning), or curriculum (e.g., 156 findings related back to extract of curriculum documentation or analysis of how curriculum 157 extracts have been applied in practice using technology). In order to capture the outcomes of this 158 screening phase, a similar technique to Araujo, Mesquita, and Hastie (2014) was employed 159 whereby a formal quality score for each study was completed on a two point scale by assessing 160 the paper value of 0 (none present or inadequately described) or 1 (present and explicitly 161 described) in relation to each of the following areas described by Cushion et al. (2010) and 162 Cushion and Townsend (2019): (a) the appropriateness of the paper focus for answering the 163 review question (i.e. topic relevance), (b) the trustworthiness of the results assessed by the 164 quality of the study (i.e. methodological and theoretical rigour), (c) appropriateness of the study 165for addressing the research question (i.e. relevance). through our discussion of 178 technology enhancements in teaching, learning and curriculum. 179 Technological enhancement in teaching: Using technology as a substitute of teachers but not 180 as transforming teaching and learning practices 181 Technology was largely seen as a support and a substitute in relation to enhancing existing 182 teaching practices in PE. Technology was closely reported in line with what students had learnt 183 because of the use of technology in teaching. The technologies that were claimed to enhance 184 teaching varied from videos to exergames, apps, and tablets. They were used mainly in 185 elementary education, but also with secondary and post-secondary samples. The most prevalent 186 of these were apps followed by exergames and videos. Aspects of teaching that were claimed to 187 be enhanced by technology included areas such as video-feedback and performance 188 (Kretschmann, 2017; Palao et al., 2015), the ability to create new cultures for students (Andre & 189 Hastie, 2018), and the direction of learning (Maivorsdotter & Quennerstedt, 2019). Some of 190 these technological enhancements were linked to the ways that teachers could harness the use of 191 technology towards assessment purposes. Studies that had a key teaching component to them 192 tended to explore how the technology was implemented into the PE lesson or course in terms of 193 the methodology of the study but then tended to focus more on the outcomes for students rather 194 than the teachers themselves. For example, Lee and Gao (2020) reported on the variables in 195 terms of students' physical activity, Lindburg et al. (2016) discussed student engagement 196 alongside variations in heart rate and Segura-Robles et al. (2020) focused on student satisfaction 197 and motivation. It is interesting therefore, that when technology is viewed towards enhancements 198 in teaching, we are more likely to see a focus on bringing about a change in terms of students' 199 learning that was not already there, rather than say a change in pedagogical approach, 200 instructional strategies, philosophies or critical thinking. 201 Technological enhancement in learning: Using technology to improve motor skills, health and 202 motivation 203 Several different types of technology were beneficial for enhancing student learning (e.g. 204 videos, exergames, apps, wearables, activity monitors or websites). Whilst technology was 205 explored in relation to learning in a variety of ways, some of the most prevalent outcomes was to 206 enhance students' health/physical aspects of learning or on motivational related outcomes. For 207 example, McGann et al. (2020) reported on how students made significant improvements in 208 locomotor skills when using exergames, whereas Potdevin et al. (2018) and Palao et al. (2015) 209 found that students made significant progress in their motor skill or athletics development and 210 self-assessment ability when using video-feedback. Enhancements in learning were largely 211 viewed from the perspective of learning in the physical domain or enhancing areas such as motor 212 competence (Kretschmann, 2017). In relation to health-related aspects, technology in the form of 213 exergames was reported to enhance students' self-esteem or mood (Andrade et al., 2020), 214 knowledge of step count and calorie burning targets provided by a wearable fitness device 215 encouraged young people to do more physical activity (Goodyear, Kerner, & Quennerstedt, 216 2017), or knowledge of energy balance and healthy diets (Chen et al., 2016).

Technological enhancement in curriculum: Using technology to facilitate the enactment of229 new curriculum 230 The use of technology to enhance either the application, development or understanding of 231 the curriculum would not seem to be a pertinent area of focus in the PE literature studies 232 included in this review. Only Calderón and Tannehill (2020) presented a proposal where, a 233 sample of PE teachers, used an ad hoc designed mobile app, to facilitate the enactment of a new 234 curriculum framework. They reported that the engagement in a learning community of inquiry 235 was paramount to these teachers' development of effective practices when enacting a new 236 models-based curriculum enhanced using one mobile app (Calderón & Tannehill, 2020). It 237 seemed that whilst the papers may be implicitly reflecting on how the technology enhancements 238 might impact on curriculum, the main focuses were on the students' learning aspect of pedagogy. 239 In addition, when looking at the curriculum contexts studies were mainly emanating out of 240 Europe followed by Asia, the USA and the UK. It presented how technology was largely seen to enhance students' 245 learning in relation to both health and motivational variables. (2019), would be two examples of technology enhancing 280 student's enjoyment and cooperation respectively, despite the TEL intervention was not 281 intentionally designed with that purpose. Furthermore, it is encouraging to see the 291 extent to which certain refined exergames could enhance the user's play experience (McGann et 292 al., 2020), or the way the pedagogical use of certain apps can enrich a debate of ideas to enhance 293 students' shared understanding of tactical concepts (Koekoek et al., 2019). It is perhaps surprising to see such a gap in studies exploring technologies enhancement 311 of curriculum in PE. As Araujo et al. (2020) argue, educators and policy makers in the field of 312 PE are still adjusting local curricula to reflect the different technological changes and there 313 remains a lack of knowledge in how these digital developments have been undertaken in 314 different contexts. It would subsequently seem that how digital technologies are incorporated 315 into, interpreted through, and help inform the field's understanding of PE curricula is still an 316 important aspect for future research. In thinking about future research in terms of exploring TEL 317 and indeed in PE, experimenting with, developing and reflecting on the use of technology-318 enhanced pedagogy or what Passey (2019) recently termed technology-enhanced education 319 would allow for researchers and educators to seek to broaden out the investigation of technology 320 and the often overlapping areas of teaching, learning, and curriculum that underpin its use. We 321 are conscious and acknowledge certain limitations of this review. These include our 322 interpretation and judgement of the quality criteria used to review the studies, the incorporation 323 of studies in languages other than English or Spanish, database/full text access, or books and 324 conference papers. Furthermore, the exclusion of papers focusing on completely online PE is a 325 limitation. That being said, we aware of recent literature from Goodyear et al. (2021) that 326 somewhat addresses this gap in knowledge. Despite these, we embrace the idea of, and related 327 research about online-only PE. We believe that there is still a large research arena to explore the 328 realities of digital technology for teaching and learning in regular (and blended) PE. Future 329 research that explores a greater diversity of curriculum contexts and technologies would also 330 allow for a broader perspective on how the use of these technologies can be adapted. By seeking 331 to deploy pedagogical approaches that attempt to incorporate technology within their core design 332 is key. Another area which could be worrying and promising at the same time would be the use 333 of virtual worlds as arenas for embodied experiential learning to happen (Loke & Golding, 334 2016). Currently, many studies advocate for the use of teaching and learning approaches based 335 on virtual worlds as powerful experiences that benefit students' learning and disciplinary 336 understanding (Pellas & Mystakidis, 2020). As a backdrop to this review, the context of the COVID-19 pandemic is likely to have353 spurred the field even further to reflect upon what the current state and use of technology within 354 pedagogy has been and where it could be when the schooling environment is augmented. Indeed, 355 the boundaries of the gymnasium or sports field can be expanded with digital technology whilst 356 exacerbating digital inequalities. A better understanding and picture of the small ways in which 357 different types of technology can be used to enhance areas of teaching and learning is being 358 developed. An area that very little was reported on a decade ago. Yet now, more than ever, 359 adopting Casey et al.'s (2017) advice to be braver and bolder in critical thought regarding what 360 outcomes are being sought to enhance through the use of technology and planning aligned 361 teaching and learning experiences accordingly.
